q: Training runs above 10^26 FLOP should require pre-registration with a public regulator before they begin.
r: Training runs above 10^26 FLOP should not require pre-registration with a regulator.
p: Anyone planning a 10^26 FLOP run should have to register it publicly first.

q: Compute thresholds are already obsolete as a regulatory trigger because algorithmic efficiency lets small runs match old frontier capability.
r: Compute thresholds remain a useful regulatory trigger despite algorithmic efficiency gains.
x: durability of compute as a proxy
p: Efficiency gains have made FLOP thresholds a useless line to regulate around.

q: Export controls on advanced AI chips to China should be tightened further even if this accelerates China's domestic chip industry.
r: Export controls on advanced AI chips to China should be relaxed because they accelerate China's domestic chip industry.
p: Chip controls on China should get stricter, even knowing they spur China's own chipmaking.

q: Cloud providers should not be required to know or report who is renting frontier-scale compute clusters.
r: Cloud providers should be required to know and report who is renting frontier-scale compute clusters.
p: Renting a giant cluster should not come with identity checks and reporting.

q: Cloud providers should be required to report to a regulator any customer assembling a cluster capable of a 10^26 FLOP training run within three months.
r: Cloud providers should not be required to report customers assembling clusters capable of 10^26 FLOP training runs.
p: Cloud firms should flag anyone assembling frontier-scale compute to the regulator.

q: Governments should abandon compute governance entirely and regulate only deployed applications.
r: Governments should keep compute governance alongside regulation of deployed applications.
p: Stop regulating compute; regulate what gets deployed and nothing upstream.

q: Advanced AI chips should be required to include hardware-level mechanisms that let regulators verify what they are being used for.
r: Advanced AI chips should not be required to include hardware-level mechanisms for regulatory verification of use.
p: Frontier chips should ship with built-in features that let regulators check their use.

q: Compute governance gives incumbent labs a permanent advantage and does more harm to competition than good for safety.
r: Compute governance does more good for safety than harm to competition, even if it advantages incumbents.
x: competition cost versus safety benefit of compute rules
p: Regulating compute mostly locks in the big labs; the safety gains do not make up for it.

q: Frontier compute clusters above a national-security threshold should be subject to on-site government inspection.
r: Frontier compute clusters should not be subject to on-site government inspection.
p: Big enough clusters should be open to government inspectors walking the floor.

q: Chip export controls should be lifted for allied and neutral countries with no tiering, letting companies sell freely outside a short list of adversaries.
r: Chip export controls should keep a tiered structure that limits sales even to many allied and neutral countries.
p: Sell chips freely to everyone but a handful of adversaries; drop the tiers.

q: Governments should cap the total compute any single company may control, even if this slows the leading labs.
r: Governments should not cap the total compute a single company may control.
p: There should be a legal ceiling on how much compute one company can own.

q: Power availability, not chip supply, will be the binding constraint on frontier training compute through 2030.
r: Chip supply, not power availability, will be the binding constraint on frontier training compute through 2030.
p: Through 2030, electricity will limit frontier training before chips do.

q: Companies should be free to build frontier data centers in any allied country without their home government's approval.
r: Companies should need home-government approval to build frontier data centers in other countries, even allied ones.
p: Siting a frontier data center in an ally's territory should not need permission from home.

q: An international agency should hold the authority to license training runs above an agreed compute threshold.
r: No international agency should hold authority to license training runs.
p: Licensing the biggest training runs should be an international agency's job.

q: Compute thresholds written into law should be indexed to algorithmic progress automatically rather than fixed at a number.
r: Compute thresholds written into law should be fixed at a number and changed only by new legislation.
p: Statutory FLOP lines should move automatically with efficiency gains.

q: Governments should require a share of new frontier data center capacity to be reserved for public-interest and academic research.
r: Governments should not require any share of new frontier data center capacity to be reserved for public-interest or academic research.
p: A slice of every new frontier data center should be earmarked for academic and public use.

q: Export controls on AI chips have failed and should be replaced with an open market plus targeted end-use enforcement.
r: Export controls on AI chips have worked well enough to keep rather than replace with an open market.
p: Chip export controls have flopped; open the market and police end uses instead.

q: Any single training run consuming more than one gigawatt of power should require a public environmental and security review before it starts.
r: Training runs consuming more than one gigawatt of power should not require a public environmental and security review.
p: A gigawatt training run should not start without a public review.

q: Governments should not subsidize domestic chip fabrication; AI hardware should be sourced wherever it is cheapest.
r: Governments should subsidize domestic chip fabrication rather than source AI hardware wherever it is cheapest.
p: Buy chips where they are cheapest; do not subsidize fabs at home.

q: Frontier labs should be required to publish their total training and inference compute use annually.
r: Frontier labs should not be required to publish their total compute use.
p: Labs should report how much compute they burn each year, training and inference.

q: Inference compute will exceed training compute as the dominant driver of frontier AI capability by 2028.
r: Training compute will remain the dominant driver of frontier AI capability through 2028, ahead of inference compute.
p: By 2028, spending compute at inference time will matter more than spending it on training.

q: Smuggling of AI chips is a minor problem that does not justify intrusive tracking of chip shipments.
r: Smuggling of AI chips is a serious enough problem to justify intrusive tracking of chip shipments.
p: Chip smuggling is small potatoes; shipment tracking is overkill.

q: Governments should have the power to commandeer private frontier compute in a declared national emergency.
r: Governments should not have the power to commandeer private frontier compute even in a declared national emergency.
p: In an emergency, the state should be able to take over private frontier compute.

q: The AI diffusion benefits of selling chips broadly outweigh the security benefits of restricting them.
r: The security benefits of restricting chip sales outweigh the AI diffusion benefits of selling them broadly.
x: diffusion versus security in chip policy
p: Spreading chips widely does more good than restricting them does for security.

q: Datacenter operators should be required to keep tamper-evident logs of which models were trained on their hardware, available to regulators on request.
r: Datacenter operators should not be required to log which models were trained on their hardware.
p: Data centers should keep sealed records of every model trained on their machines.

q: Startups should be exempt from all compute reporting requirements until they have raised more than $1 billion.
r: Startups should be subject to compute reporting requirements regardless of how much they have raised.
p: Until a startup has raised a billion dollars, compute reporting rules should not apply to it.

q: A global agreement should cap the largest permitted training run at 10^28 FLOP until international verification tools exist.
r: There should be no global cap on training run size pending international verification tools.
p: Until we can verify each other's runs, the world should agree to stop at 10^28 FLOP.

q: Compute should be treated like electricity: a utility available to anyone who pays, with no scrutiny of what they do with it.
r: Compute should not be treated like a utility; large purchases warrant scrutiny of intended use.
p: Compute is a commodity like power; sell it to anyone and ask no questions.

q: By 2028, two companies will control the majority of the world's frontier-class AI compute.
r: By 2028, frontier-class AI compute will remain spread across more than a handful of companies rather than concentrated in two.
p: Two firms will own most of the world's frontier compute by 2028.

q: Any AI chip sale above $100 million should require the buyer to accept remote attestation that the chips are located where declared.
r: AI chip sales above $100 million should not require buyers to accept remote location attestation.
p: Big chip buyers should have to prove, remotely, that the chips are where they said.
